claims.text: Adding a specific minor element can improve the strength–plasticity combination of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed intervention applies to an as-cast refractory high-entropy alloy.
The intervention is the addition of boron or carbon as a minor alloying element.
The predicted benefit should occur under standard processing conditions and room-temperature testing.
The minor element alters grain-boundary structure.
The minor element alters grain-boundary composition.
The altered grain boundaries enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
The altered grain boundaries enhance grain-boundary sliding.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion and sliding improve plasticity without compromising strength.
The modified alloy will have 20% greater tensile ductility than an otherwise comparable alloy without the minor-element addition.
The modified alloy will have 10% greater yield strength than an otherwise comparable alloy without the minor-element addition.
The expected improvement is limited to a specific range of alloy compositions and processing conditions.
The optimal identity and amount of the minor-element addition are not well understood.
The underlying mechanisms are not well understood.
The hypothesis is to be tested by tensile testing matched alloys with and without the minor-element addition.
Failure of the modified alloy to show a significant strength–plasticity improvement relative to the reference alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes addition of a specific minor element, but the intervention gives two alternatives, boron or carbon, rather than one specified intervention.
The mechanism is stated affirmatively as enhanced grain-boundary cohesion and sliding, while the uncertainty field says the underlying mechanisms are not well understood.
